articles.title_zh: Dennis Haskins, Mr. Belding on ‘Saved by the Bell,’ Dies at 75
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Attorney blasts Cornell over rape allegations, Jack Smith faces Senate GOP on Jan. 6 probe, and why Week 3 was one of the wildest in NFL history
Dennis Haskins, the actor best known for his role as principal Richard Belding on the high school comedy series “Saved by the Bell,” has died, his agent said Monday.
Haskins was 75. The cause and manner of death were unavailable.
“It’s a tragic loss,” Jay Schachter, head of film and television for Stewart Talent in New York City, said in a statement.
Haskins’ role on the show, which aired from 1989 to 1993, would come to define him for millions of fans.
“Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis, loved him even more,” Schachter said. “He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans.”
Haskins was born and raised in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and attended the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, where he reported for the student newspaper, acted in campus productions and was a founding member of the community theater group known as the Harlequins, according to his university biography .
As a young man, he worked as a music manager, agent and concert promoter and boasted Tom Jones and Gregg Allman among his clients, according to his IMDb bio .
Early in his career, he landed appearances on TV’s “Magnum, P.I.” and “The Twilight Zone,” according to IMDb.
His acting career was boosted by his portrayal of Mr. Belding on Disney Channel’s “Good Morning, Miss Bliss” in 1988, according to the university bio. The next year, NBC aired the show as “Saved by the Bell”; it ran until 1993.
He reprised the role on “Saved by the Bell: The New Class,” which aired Saturday mornings from 1993 to 2000 on NBC. After the show’s end, he found work in several movies and television shows, including “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia,” according to his university bio.
Schachter said Haskins will be missed.
“He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly,” he said. “I’m heartbroken.”
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Emmy Beck-Aden is an associate booking producer for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: America's Canadian import restrictions come into force. Here are the products barred from entry
articles.title_zh: America's Canadian import restrictions come into force. Here are the products barred from entry
articles.content_orig:
The White House banned imports of some Canadian vehicles, dairy and alcohol products on Tuesday, as officials sent mixed signals on the prospect of a trade deal.
The long list of impacted goods includes motorcycles and mopeds with petrol engines larger than 800cc, whey products and molasses , and a slew of alcoholic beverages — mainly those packaged for direct consumption — from beer and cider to wine, whiskey and vodka.
The products are estimated to total around $19.9 billion of Canadian imports by the American Action Forum .
The import ban, announced earlier this month by the Trump administration, is the latest step in a war of words — and tit-for-tat tariffs — between the U.S. and Canada.
President Donald Trump said on Monday he expected a "fair deal" with Canada within the coming weeks, but continued to strike a combative tone.
"They take advantage of us, they feel entitled ... there's nothing they have that we need," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
"I think what's going to happen is over the next three to four weeks they're going to come to us and they're going to say, 'We're going to get rid of all the tariffs.' We're going to win everything," Trump said.
However, officials suggest little progress towards a deal.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that there was "no urgency on our side" to strike an agreement and noted that the U.S. still had "a lot of other trade" with Canada.
"We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things ... so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," Greer said.
Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told a press conference on Friday that the U.S. was "imposing illegal and unjustified tariffs on sectors of our economy that are causing considerable hardship to businesses and workers across the country."
LeBlanc said the countries were "talking about trying to find alternatives to the current circumstances" but  that they were "not going to sign a deal that's bad for Canada."
"We have said we will sign an agreement when we think there is one that is in the interests of Canada's sovereignty and Canada's economy... but we're not waiting by the phone," LeBlanc said.
Ottawa has stopped short of unveiling fresh retaliation since the Sept. 9 announcement of a dairy and alcohol import ban.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has meanwhile spent the month courting closer ties with the European Union as relations with the U.S. fray, suggesting in a recent speech that the White House is "weaponizing" economic policy as a form of "coercion" on other nations.
Canada has imposed tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on CA$27.6 billion worth of a slew of U.S. goods, including steel, dairy, agricultural equipment, paper, household appliances, furniture, clothing and electronics.
It said these were a "dollar for dollar" response to Washington's 50% tariffs on goods including cement, wine, hockey sticks and more, imposed in August.
The measures target a relatively small portion of the annual $715.5 billion trade in goods between the countries, but continued escalation or a prolonged stand-off are expected to significantly impact sectors such as metals and autos , and hurt small and medium-sized businesses on both sides of the border.
The Bank of Canada warned this month that new tariffs had made the country's growth prospects more uncertain and increased upside risks to inflation.

British counterterrorism police are leading an investigation after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and preparing a terrorist act near an air base used by U.S. forces.
Police received a report at around 12:45 a.m. Sunday about three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. Armed officers responded and arrested the men in nearby Whelford.
Fairford is used as a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. The base has hosted U.S. B-52 and B-1 bombers during the Iran war , according to ABC News . American forces have used Fairford to carry out strikes against Iranian missile sites, the Associated Press reported.
Read More: Why More Republicans Are Breaking With Trump on Iran
In a press conference Sunday, Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said that about 85 households in the area were advised to evacuate early Sunday morning as a precaution.
"A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles, while the Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit examine them,” Ocone said. A statement from police earlier Sunday said that they believe the situation is “contained.”
Aerial footage from Sky News shows a bomb disposal robot moving between three white vans at the site, with the rear doors of two vehicles open.
Ocone added that the men remain in custody and will be questioned by police.
The base is home to both the 501st Combat Support Wing Headquarters and the 420th Air Base Squadron, and serves as the “preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe,” according to the U.S. Air Force.
TIME has reached out to the U.S. Air Force for comment on the incident.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who assumed the post in July, called the incident “deeply concerning” on X .
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” he wrote. “The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.” When asked by reporters about the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump called them “fantastic.” “They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” Trump said of the suspects, “and working with the British worked out great.”
Trump also said the suspects had been under surveillance before their arrests. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said.
British police have not confirmed that RAF Fairford was the intended target of the suspected attacks. The Associated Press reported that investigators were considering a possible connection to Iran, but no such link has been confirmed.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO document
articles.title_zh: Anthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO document
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic plans to warn speculative investors in its IPO prospectus that its AI models pose a "catastrophic or existential risk to humanity," several reports said on Tuesday.
The company, which is gearing up for a much-anticipated IPO , dedicated over a third of its IPO filing, or around 80 of 261 pages, to laying out the potential risks of the technology it's developing and is seeking investment for, according to a report from Reuters . It only used 48 pages to discuss its actual business.
The five-year-old company, known for its frontier language model Claude, warned that AI can have "self-preserving behaviors," including being able to "resist shutdown," "conceal or manipulate information," and carry out behaviors "resembling blackmail," per the Reuters report.
The company is pursuing a $2 trillion valuation when it goes public and reported in the filing that it made a net loss of $42 billion in 2025. It's planning to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing, and other infrastructure in the coming year, according to Reuters.
Anthropic also warned that its customer base is extremely narrow, with nearly a quarter of its revenue last year coming from just two clients, two people familiar with the filing told the Financial Times .
Anthropic's co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei has previously written various essays warning on the threats of AI, including saying the technology will cause "unusually painful" disruption to the job market .
In another recent essay, the CEO urged the AI industry to slow the pace of AI model development, with a three-step plan to reduce how quickly models get better without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI."
Those calls for a slowdown are somewhat of a "head scratcher" for the sector, to which the market has reacted "pretty resoundingly," Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives told CNBC earlier today.
"You need guardrails from a safety perspective, but the fact for Anthropic and OpenAI to slow down, if they slowed down, China would just accelerate and win, and I think that's part of this quagmire that you're seeing is that there's some regulatory capture going on. There's definitely a game of poker, but for Anthropic, they got to continue to put foot on the pedal."
Ives added that while guardrails are essential, regulation could stifle innovation. That continues to be the "biggest concern within the U.S., which is why we're in an F1 race," he said.

articles.title_orig: Smart ring maker Oura postpones IPO due to market 'uncertainty'
articles.title_zh: Smart ring maker Oura postpones IPO due to market 'uncertainty'
articles.content_orig:
Oura has said that it is delaying plans for its public listing on the Nasdaq due to uncertainty in the IPO market.
The delay comes despite "strong demand" and a strengthening of the business since the start of the IPO process, the company said in a statement on Tuesday.
The company, which makes a smart ring that tracks wearers' health and sleep, formally launched its IPO plans just last week on Sept. 21.
At the time, the company planned to raise up to $2.2 billion with the sale of 50 million shares.
"Our mission is to empower people to live healthier, longer, and an IPO is just one step in our journey," said CEO Tom Hale on Tuesday.
"We aim to deliver an extraordinary IPO for our employees and investors and we have the luxury of choosing our moment ," he added . "In the meantime, we will execute against the opportunities ahead."
Oura is profitable, the company said, with revenue expected to grow 90% year over year for the fiscal year 2026.
Launched in 2015, Oura's smart ring has evolved well beyond sleep tracking and now features a variety of features focused on broader health and wellness. In recent years, it has increasingly focused on advancing preventative health through new capabilities, AI, analytics and other features.
Oura is the latest U.S. public market hopeful to delay an IPO in recent weeks. Holtec Nuclear withdrew its IPO earlier this month citing adverse market sentiment in equity markets.
Holtec said that uncertainty over data development compounded "pre-existing headwinds, including rising energy costs, elevated global trade tensions, ongoing military conflicts, and mounting inflation fears that have driven the central banks of major economies (EU, Japan and US) to raise their benchmark rates."

articles.title_orig: Senate GOP to press Jack Smith on Trump Jan. 6 probe as DOJ targets investigators
articles.title_zh: Senate GOP to press Jack Smith on Trump Jan. 6 probe as DOJ targets investigators
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Attorney blasts Cornell over rape allegations, Jack Smith faces Senate GOP on Jan. 6 probe, and why Week 3 was one of the wildest in NFL history
WASHINGTON — Former special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two since-dismissed federal criminal cases against Donald Trump, is expected to face questions on Tuesday from the president’s allies in the Senate about his handling of his investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol .
Smith is set to testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee amid the Justice Department’s push to target law enforcement officials involved with Smith’s investigation into Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election results as well as the probe into his handling of classified documents after he left office in January 2021.
Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, has repeatedly criticized Smith. The title of Tuesday’s hearing, which Grassley will chair — “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans and Related Matters” — suggests a potentially combative hearing. With it, Grassley asserts that Smith misused his investigative powers and politically targeted Republicans. Smith, who as a career prosecutor went after Republicans and Democrats, has denied such allegations.
Grassley said in a statement ahead of the hearing that Smith “must answer” for what the senator portrays as “rampant abuse of authority and political targeting” funded by American taxpayers.
“If Jack Smith did that to Democrats, you’d never hear the end of it,” Grassley said in the statement, adding that his goal is holding accountable the Justice Department for actions taken during the Biden administration.
Smith did not issue a statement in advance of his testimony.
Smith has said he believes a jury would have convicted Trump in the 2020 election-related case had it gone to trial and that the notion that his decisions were “ influenced or directed by the Biden administration or other political actors is, in a word, laughable .” Smith’s final report in the election interference case stated that Trump “ inspired his supporters to commit acts of physical violence ” at the Capitol on Jan. 6.
Trump pleaded not guilty in Smith’s Jan. 6 case and denied after the attack that he incited his supporters, calling his remarks at a rally that day “totally appropriate.” Trump later described Jan. 6 defendants as “hostages” and gave them mass clemency upon his return to office.
The Trump administration last year launched a so-called grand conspiracy investigation looking at actions taken by federal law enforcement officials dating back to 2016, which would fall outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes .
The Trump administration also has purged FBI and Justice Department officials involved in past Trump investigations. Defense attorneys for current and former officials informed a court last week that DOJ officials appear interested in probing the circumstances of an August 2022 FBI search of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, during which agents found classified documents that were at the heart of one of the since-dismissed Trump cases.
Joe diGenova, who was a federal prosecutor during Ronald Reagan’s presidency, headed up the “grand conspiracy” investigation until he left the Justice Department this month. He told NBC News that “ lanes got crossed ” in his final days.
In his first public testimony before Congress earlier this year, Smith told the House Judiciary Committee that he would not be intimidated and predicted that the Trump administration would attempt to launch a criminal case against him. Months later, one of Trump’s allies on Capitol Hill, Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, asked the Trump administration to investigate Jordan’s assertion that Smith “seemingly” made false statements in congressional testimony.
Smith’s lawyers said he provided “truthful, responsive answers” and that Jordan’s referral “reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.” Former federal prosecutors have told NBC News that the Justice Department would have a tough time bringing a perjury case against Smith.
Smith is not expected to discuss the classified documents investigation because Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon ordered that that portion of his report as special counsel cannot be released. The Justice Department has taken the position that answering questions about that investigation would violate Cannon’s order.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Reportedly Cancels GPT-6.1 Astra's Release Over Deceptive Behavior
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Reportedly Cancels GPT-6.1 Astra's Release Over Deceptive Behavior
articles.content_orig:
It was supposed to debut in October, but it apparently showed higher levels of deception than previous models.
OpenAI has canceled the release of its new model, GPT-6.1 Astra, according to The Wall Street Journal . It was due for launch in October and was going to debut inside ChatGPT and Codex, but it reportedly showed higher levels of deception than its predecessors during internal testing. Saachi Jain, who leaves OpenAI's safety training, said that GPT-6.1 Astra performed poorly on tests that measure how well it adheres to instructions. It also wasn't honest about telling testers the actions it did and didn't perform in order to achieve its goal.
In addition, the model would take actions to accomplish tasks without asking for permission, such as using external tools and services. Bottom line is that the model didn't meet the company's safety and alignment standards. After the Hugging Face incident came to light, OpenAI had admitted that its models were involved in several other events wherein they had escaped their isolated testing environments to break into third party websites and services.
Just last week, the company told The New York Times that its agents had targeted a Commerce Department and a Securities and Exchange Commission website. It also told the publication that it was investigating a supposed incident involving a website operated by the Department of Education. Before that, and in addition to OpenAI's agents hacking into Hugging Face, its agents also broke into Australia's Medicare public health insurance system, a community-ran packaging service for Ruby programs and a German coding forum . The company revealed, as well, that it found more than 50 instances of its agents posting ChatGPT user-provided images to photo-sharing websites.
OpenAI, along with Anthropic, has been calling for an industry-wide slowdown of frontier AI development. "We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," OpenAI previously wrote in a misalignment report. Florida attorney general James Uthmeier petitioned a state court to prevent OpenAI from training new models without independent oversight. "If Sam Altman meant what he said about slowing down, he can join our ask to the court," he said.
The company will still use the same base model for future generations of GPT-6, even though GPT-6.1 Astra has already been scrapped. It will conduct an investigation to identify the root cause of the problems found in the model, Jain said, and will employ reinforcement learning that rewards the correct behavior.

articles.title_orig: News organizations ask court to bar White House enforcement of access ban
articles.title_zh: News organizations ask court to bar White House enforcement of access ban
articles.content_orig:
A logo on a booth for CNN is seen in the press area at the White House, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Washington. Rod Lamkey/AP hide caption
Three news outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banished from White House grounds this month asked a federal court to block the ban until the case is resolved, saying the administration has "persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban" despite a judge's restraining order — including selectively barring CNN from White House pool duties.
"The White House's words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity," lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico wrote in a filing late Monday.
"Because the ban is an unlawful assault on the most fundamental First Amendment freedoms and will inflict irreparable harm on Plaintiffs and the public if not restrained, this Court should preliminarily enjoin its enforcement pending the resolution of this case," the filing said.
It was the latest development in the back-and-forth saga of the Trump administration and the news media during the second term of his presidency. It has been a contentious relationship that has raised multiple First Amendment questions, produced sanctions and restrictions on White House and Pentagon reporters and led to several lawsuits that are winding their ways through the federal court system.
A two-week temporary restraining order on Trump's ban of the three organizations, issued by U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly last week, restored the outlets' White House access, but expires Oct. 8. The preliminary injunction requested in Monday's filing would extend the White House access until the case is finally resolved.
In a statement emailed to The Associated Press immediately after the filing, the lead attorney for the three news outlets called the ban "a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process."
"The president and his administration have continued to make clear that this ban has only one purpose: to punish reporting he doesn't like," said the lawyer, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr.
"That's retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, pure and simple," Boutrous said. "With the district court's temporary restraining order expiring this week, it is critical to ensure that the White House continues to be prevented from implementing this unconstitutional ban on the free press."
The filing came a day after the Trump administration made clear it was not backing down from its contention that the sudden ban, which began Sept. 19, was justified.
"When it comes to the White House, it is the people's house," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on ABC on Sunday, invoking an argument the administration has made since the beginning. "It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there."
Monday's 42-page filing reiterated many of the arguments that the news outlets made in their original lawsuit against Trump and the White House, filed two days after the reporters were banned.
It also added mention of the White House broadcast pool rotation, which has become a battleground in the last few days in the standoff between Trump and the media.
The White House, it said, "has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on Sept. 26 — to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public."
When the ban was implemented, CNN was removed from its duties as part of the broadcast pool, which consists of the five main networks: CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. In solidarity, the other networks decided to suspend the pool until CNN was allowed back in.
On Friday, CNN was allowed to cover the president with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the National Archives. But in a new setback Saturday, the White House banned the network from Air Force One, preventing it from covering Trump's trip to a college football game in Tennessee. The rest of the pool declined to provide a replacement, in solidarity with CNN.
Blanche defended that decision, too. "The president has every right to decide who gets to fly on his plane," he said in the Sunday interview. He added that Trump was "sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news." He added that news coverage he described as "misinformation" amounted to a national security issue.
"That is what is a national security problem, when you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House," he said.
Kelly threw cold water on that argument in his ruling last week granting the temporary restraining order against the White House ban. "The court is skeptical … that defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation" for removal of access, Kelly wrote.
His ruling did not directly address the TV pool rotation. In the new filing, the plaintiffs describe the important function the pool provides and makes the case that it's an important part of the regular access to the president, and his activities, that the media has traditionally had — and must be restored.
It singles out the Air Force One case. "CNN received no official communication from the White House explaining its exclusion," the filing says. "Because CNN was excluded and no replacement designated, no primary television network pooler accompanied the President on the trip."
For now, networks in the pool have decided to address the ongoing standoff on a case-by-case basis, according to a person familiar with the pool's operation, speaking on condition of anonymity to give details of ongoing discussions.
On Sunday, Fox covered a pool event; on Monday, NBC was covering the president in the Oval Office. CNN is not in the rotation until Thursday. If the network is again barred from a pool event, the networks will decide together, presumably based on the newsworthiness of the situation, whether to provide a replacement or to refrain from coverage as they did previously.
The issues at stake are difficult. On the one hand, the networks want to take a stand on behalf of press freedom and against efforts to intimidate coverage. On the other, media outlets have an obvious purpose of providing news to their audiences.
"There are not a lot of good options," said David A. Schulz, director of the Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.
Should the White House continue to bar CNN, Schulz said, networks may choose "to exert their market power and say, 'We're not going to play ball with you.'"
The question, Schulz added, is: "Who's going to back down first?"
The networks "may well feel like they're between a rock and a hard place," noted RonNell Andersen Jones, a law professor at the University of Utah.
"Capitulation might be perceived as abandonment of core components of press freedom," Andersen Jones said. "But the practicalities of lengthy White House news blackouts are also complicated, and refusing to cover major news at the highest levels of government might itself feel like a failure to serve the goals of democracy."

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Rise as U.S.-Iran Talks Remain Uncertain
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Rise as U.S.-Iran Talks Remain Uncertain
articles.content_orig:
If you think your energy costs are high now, the situation may be about to get a whole lot worse.
With traffic in the Strait of Hormuz – normally the primary route for oil leaving the Middle East – hovering below 15% of prewar levels , oil prices have increased from US$65 a barrel before the conflict in Iran began in February 2026 to more than $100 a barrel in mid-September.
When the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran, analysts feared prices would soon reach $150 or even $200 a barrel. That hasn’t happened yet. But seven months into the conflict, with no clear end in sight, the global oil market has now largely exhausted the safety measures that exist to keep a lid on petroleum prices.
As researchers who study the relationship between energy and national security , we have been following these dynamics throughout the conflict, and the oil market is now showing signs that significant price hikes – and perhaps even shortages – may be on the way.
Some oil has been able to make it out of the Persian Gulf despite the closure of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia increased output via its East-West pipeline , which runs from Abqaiq on the Persian Gulf overland to Yanbu on the coast of the Red Sea. At full capacity, that pipeline can carry as much as 7 million barrels per day , although only about 4 million to 5 million barrels per day are typically exported.
But attacks on the pipeline in mid-September that Saudi Arabia blames on Iran-backed militias based in Iraq forced the Saudis to temporarily halt oil shipments through that pipeline. The pipeline has now restarted operations at very low volumes, but it will likely take at least six to eight weeks to regain full capacity. Even this short cessation has tightened already constrained oil markets, and the threat of further Houthi attacks on Red Sea oil exports will only add to inflationary pressures.
Meanwhile, in Russia, Ukrainian drone attacks have damaged refineries , reducing Russian production of diesel fuel and prompting the country to ban exports of it . That has removed another 3% of the global daily supply of diesel, an important fuel for trucking and shipping . When diesel costs go up, the result is inflation in the cost of goods across the global economy.
In the U.S., 47 states experienced record-high diesel prices on Sept. 22, with the national average reaching $6.52 per gallon.
The high prices prompted President Donald Trump to threaten to ban diesel exports , a move analysts suggest would make matters worse by accentuating global supply shortages and driving world prices upward .
Beyond diesel, motor oil prices have quadrupled , and supply shortages are starting to take hold. For instance, Costco has almost doubled its prices for motor oil and has limited the amount customers can buy.
The upshot from all this is that Americans are spending a lot more on fuel in 2026 as compared to 2025. Between March 1 and late September, Americans spent an additional $72 billion on gasoline compared to the same period a year ago, as well as $45 billion more on diesel.  That’s $117 billion in additional fuel costs, above and beyond the costs of the war itself, which the Pentagon estimated at $45 billion as of early September.
These shocks are even more acute outside the United States, which is the world’s largest energy producer. South and Southeast Asian countries, which were more reliant on imports from the Persian Gulf than the United States, were hit hard soon after the war broke out. Some of them have had to ration fuel , while others enacted emergency measures like shortening the work or school week to reduce fuel use .
These challenges are now hitting Europe hard as well. On Sept. 20, some 15% of French service stations had reportedly run out of either diesel or gas .
The international community has already taken most of the measures available to curb oil demand and boost its supply. Those moves have reduced the scale of oil price increases, but they did not prevent them entirely. Now, the toolbox is largely empty, leaving prices on the brink of spiking again.
In March 2026, a coordinated effort among 32 countries released more than 400 million barrels of oil into the global market from those countries’ strategic reserves. Those stockpiles are now substantially depleted, and it is not clear how much additional oil that countries will be willing or even able to release as the war continues.
Since the war began, the United States alone has released 130 million barrels , leaving its reserves at a 40-year low . The U.S. may not be able to release much more without compromising the structural integrity of the salt caverns where the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is stored.
China has played the largest role in containing global oil prices to date by releasing official reserves as well as what now seem to be massive additional reserves not previously disclosed to the public . The country reduced its crude oil imports by nearly 50% between February and June 2026.
The increased electrification of the Chinese economy played a key role in reducing Chinese demand for oil during this period. More than 60% of new passenger car sales in China are electric vehicles or plug-in hybrids, and 30% of its heavy truck sales are now electric.
Overall, China’s electrification of its transport sector allowed it to reduce oil consumption by 1.35 million barrels per day in the first half of 2026.
Other countries are looking to China for help as well. The country’s international sales of electric vehicles, batteries and solar panels have skyrocketed , as other countries seek to insulate themselves from oil market shocks.
Less encouragingly when it comes to greenhouse gas emissions, China has used more coal to offset oil demand and as an alternative means of petrochemical production as well.
Of perhaps more immediate concern, China’s oil demand is now starting to creep up again, with crude imports rising 6.2% in August 2026 as compared with the previous month. Even if its imports don’t reach prewar levels any time soon, increased Chinese demand, coupled with a tighter oil market, may result in additional price hikes over the next few weeks.
China still has about four to six months of stockpiles, including commercial and strategic reserves, but Beijing may soon seek to gradually restock its inventories , although the Chinese may postpone these purchases if prices continue to soar.
Sustained conflict in Iran – itself a major oil producer – continued disruptions of oil shipments in the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran-linked militias’ disruptions to shipping in the Red Sea could mean the reemergence of the nightmare scenarios analysts envisioned when the fighting began.
It’s not clear if that would translate into simply much higher prices at the pump or turn into 1970s-style shortages , where there’s not enough fuel available at any price and lines stretch around the block at gas stations.
With the 2026 midterm elections looming, the White House will want to avoid that scenario at all costs. But the Trump administration has already released large amounts from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and has rejected policies that would have reduced oil demand, such as stricter fuel economy standards or incentives for electric vehicle adoption.
At this point, Trump has relatively few options available to blunt new price shocks, the effects of which may be visible not just at the pump but also at the ballot box.

articles.title_orig: Bears call on QB3 Case Keenum in rousing victory over Eagles
articles.title_zh: Bears call on QB3 Case Keenum in rousing victory over Eagles
articles.content_orig:
The Eagles earned poor marks across the board but Sirianni should shoulder the blame as the team's head coach against a third-string quarterback in Case Keenum.
CHICAGO — Instant grades on the Eagles’ performance in their 27-7 loss to the Chicago Bears :
Jalen Hurts started slow, rebounded after an odd series of events took him out of the game, and then folded under the weight of an overall terrible performance by the Eagles. Hurts held the ball too long once he was forced to drop to pass in the second half. After two strong outings to open the season, he took a step back.
» READ MORE: Eagles fall 27-7 in Monday night dud; Bears’ third-stringer Case Keenum throws for 247 yards, accounts for 3 TDs
Hurts was nearly picked off by former Eagle T.J. Edwards on a third-down pass to returning former Eagle Zach Ertz to open the second half. But Edwards made sure to hang on the next time the ball came his way, intercepting Hurts on a late third-quarter fourth down when the quarterback only had eyes for DeVonta Smith .
He had to leave the game for a potential concussion after Bears linebacker D’Marco Jackson nailed him out of bounds in the second quarter. While Hurts was getting checked out in the medical tent, his replacement Andy Dalton tossed an interception in the end zone.
Like the entire Eagles team, Hurts had a rough start. He committed an intentional grounding penalty on the first series and threw short of an open Saquon Barkley , who had all kinds of green in front of him, on the second series. But he bounced back, especially after the cautionary trip to the medical tent. Hurts wisely snuck in for a touchdown with the clock winding down to 1 second just before the break.
Saquon Barkley had all kinds of space and lanes to burst through on outside zone runs in the first half. He was decisive and rushed for 73 yards on 11 carries. He spun out of a would-be tackle on a 7-yard rush to open the second half, but Barkley was stifled the rest of the way and finished with 82 yards on 15 carries.
Tank Bigsby fumbled after a short catch in the first quarter, but the Bears failed to convert good field position into points. Will Shipley was often on the field on third downs and caught an 11-yard pass out of the backfield.
It’s hard to blame this group for the loss, but they didn’t do enough to offset the mistakes of others. Receiver DeVonta Smith led the Eagles with six catches for 65 yards. He made a breathtaking 30-yard grab over Bears corner Jaylon Johnson in the second quarter. He had a 13-yard catch on third down in the second quarter, and he drew a 21-yard pass interference penalty on the next play.
Makai Lemon caught a 19-yard pass at the second level on a crossing route to open the game and finished with three grabs for 29 yards. Dontayvion Wicks pulled in just 2 of 5 passes for 32 yards. He had a 19-yard reception in the third quarter.
» READ MORE: Jalen Hurts and the Eagles took a major hit against the Bears. They have to find a way to bounce back.
With tight end Dallas Goedert out with an MCL knee injury for at least the next two weeks, the Eagles brought back Zach Ertz . He was activated off the practice squad despite having just a week of practice and being less than seven months removed from knee surgery.
Ertz was occasionally the receiving tight end in 11 personnel. His first catch back in midnight green went for nine yards just before the half. Ertz missed a block on a bubble screen to Lemon.
Blocking tight end Johnny Mundt led the way on a Barkley 8-yard run in the second quarter. Elijah Moore dressed for his first game as an Eagle with Hollywood Brown out with an ankle injury. He was the motion man on several plays.
The first-half run game will have to be a silver lining. The Eagles finally got the ground game going after two miserable performances. But they struggled to counter the Bears’ second-half adjustments. The pass protection was often sound for Hurts, as it was on Hurts’ 19-yard pass to Wicks. But the offense was often out of whack in the second half.
Drew Kendall had some nice run blocks in his second start at center. He had a key block on Bears veteran defensive tackle Grady Jarrett on Barkley’s 12-yard outside zone run. Kendall did well to climb to the second level on Barkley’s 7-yard tote in the second quarter. But he had a few breakdowns, as well. Cam Jurgens looked stronger in his second career start at left guard. It helps to not have to face Jeffery Simmons. But he had errors, too, and gave up a pressure late in the second quarter.
Tackles Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata were once again the best of the unit. But when Hurts was forced to drop on almost every play as the Eagles trailed, it became too difficult to hold up. On a Barkley 17-yard rush off the right in the second quarter, Johnson had a kick-out block.
Right guard Tyler Steen had a key block on Barkley’s 17-yarder, but a holding penalty brought back a Barkley 19-yard scoot in the first quarter. Markel Bell was the sixth O-lineman on a run play that resulted in a loss.
The big storyline coming in was how the Eagles would stop a run attack that stomped all over them a year ago. They did, for the most part, as Bears running backs D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai were held to under a combined 100 yards until late in the fourth quarter. Instead, they got torched through the air by no other than Case Keenum, who hadn’t started at quarterback in nearly three years.
The D-line was solid in run defense, but they failed to get to Keenum enough and didn’t notch a sack. Jalen Carter has yet to show he’s a $152 million defensive tackle. He has a wrist injury, but he’s seemingly always banged up. Carter’s run tackle for loss in the second quarter helped keep the Bears from converting a turnover into points.
Jordan Davis didn’t record his first run tackle until the second half. Moro Ojomo had a couple pressures, but his neutral zone infraction on fourth down in the fourth quarter was an egregious mistake. Byron Young made a run stop for no gain on the Bears’ first possession.
Jonathan Greenard was active for his first game with the Eagles. He was on a pitch count after missing the first two weeks with a pectoral injury. Greenard still made his presence felt with some pressure off the edge. Jalyx Hunt is still without a sack this season. He’s played well, but can’t seem to finish. Hunt appeared to be out of his run gap on a third-down conversion in the fourth quarter. Nolan Smith Jr. was just as quiet as a pass rusher. Greenard’s presence meant that A.J. Epenesa was inactive for the first time this season.
The Eagles just didn’t do enough at the second level. Zack Baun and Jihaad Campbell led the Eagles in tackles, but they were often just cleaning up messes or missed tackles. Baun was victimized on a fourth-and-1 play-fake on the Bears’ first drive. He could have done more to bring down Luther Burden on his 8-yard catch when he kept his legs churning and muscled into the end zone later on the possession.
Campbell finished with a joint-team high nine tackles, but he struggled at times to get off blocks. The Eagles had little choice but to let Nakobe Dean walk, but his replacement has been a downgrade so far this season.
Quinyon Mitchell might have been the only Eagles defender who came to play. He deflected a fourth-down pass near the goal line in the second quarter. He later made a tackle for loss on a run play that was strung out. Mitchell broke up a third-down pass in the third quarter.
Riq Woolen had a great first two games, but he can get handsy and it cost him this week. He committed holding and illegal contact penalties in the first half. The second flag, which came on third down, was a little nitpicky. Woolen blitzed several times off the edge in the first half, but Keenum was able to take advantage with one less cornerback in coverage.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee is set to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years
articles.title_zh: Tennessee is set to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years
articles.content_orig:
People gather during a March 4 Mercy protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee State Capitol, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. ahead of the Sept. 30th scheduled execution of Christa Pike. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a classmate in a jealous rage and became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Now 50, she is scheduled to be put to death Wednesday in what would be Tennessee's first execution of a woman in 200 years.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted in the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim's body.
Pike does not deny her guilt, but her attorneys and supporters argue a death sentence is not appropriate for a crime committed at that age by a teen with untreated mental illness after a childhood of brutal sexual abuse and neglect. Slemmer's mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced Monday that he would not grant clemency. Pike's attorneys have asked the Supreme Court to stay the execution.
Pike's attorneys said she experienced an exceptionally traumatic and abusive childhood.
FILE - This undated photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike. Tennessee Department of Correction/via AP hide caption
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at ages 11 and 17. He said Pike's lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration.
Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Pike told police she initially only wanted to fight Slemmer but ended up killing her in a frenzied attack. In her clemency petition, Pike's attorneys said her untreated mental illness and background made her unable to "put the brakes on."
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime," Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.
Ferrell said more today is known about adolescent brain development and that Pike's death sentence is an outlier. He noted that Pike's boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation.
In the modern death penalty era, Ferrell said, other 18-year-olds who were sentenced to death in Tennessee have since had their sentences reduced.
The Death Penalty Information Center said 275 people nationwide have been executed for crimes they committed at age 18, 19 or 20 in the modern death penalty era, but that death sentences for those in that age group have become increasingly rare.
"If Christa Pike was tried today, I do not believe a jury that knew about the documented sexual abuse and neglect she experienced as a child would sentence her to death," Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said.
Speaking by telephone from Florida, Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, also pointed to her daughter's age and said Slemmer never got a chance to grow up.
"Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," Martinez said.
Martinez said her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers.
"She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly," Martinez said. "She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall."
She said her daughter called her from Job Corps on the night of the murder, but the call was dropping because of bad reception. When Martinez called back, her daughter had already gone out.
"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst. Colleen's birthday was last week. She would have been 51," Martinez said.
The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s. Shipp, Pike's boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body.
If Pike's execution proceeds as scheduled, it would be Tennessee's first execution of a woman since 1820, Maher said.
Executions of female inmates are also rare in the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been executed in the country, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the center.
Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman, for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government has put a female inmate to death. Georgia executed a woman in 2015.

articles.title_orig: Malaysia begins sending home Myanmar refugees despite safety concerns
articles.title_zh: Malaysia begins sending home Myanmar refugees despite safety concerns
articles.content_orig:
Malaysia has begun sending nearly 1,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, describing their return as voluntary despite warnings from the United Nations and rights groups that Myanmar remains unsafe for them.
Dozens of buses arrived under police escort at a stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia on Tuesday, the AFP news agency reported. Journalists were barred from the grounds. The passengers were expected to be processed before being taken to the base and transported to Myanmar by ship.
The Myanmar army has repeatedly cracked down on the country’s Rohingya minority, including a wave of violence in 2017 that many rights groups have described as genocide, and which set off a major refugee crisis, with hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh, Malaysia, India and other neighbouring nations. Myanmar does not officially recognise the Rohingya as an ethnic community with local roots, instead describing them as “Bengalis” — in effect, calling them Bangladeshi migrants.
As of February 2026, Malaysia had more than 126,144 Rohingya refugees. Bangladesh hosts the most Rohingya refugees — more than 1.2 million.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya, leaving a question about who is being sent back. The nearly 1,500 picked for repatriation on Tuesday are part of the group. The Ministry of Home Affairs said two Myanmar naval warships and a hospital ship would be used.
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said it had no role in the operation and warned that continuing conflict and violence in Myanmar meant conditions for safe and dignified returns did not exist. “Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision, and take place in conditions of safety and dignity,” it told the Reuters news agency.
Malaysia’s Home Ministry declined to comment on the warning, referring to its earlier statement that the returns were voluntary.
Rights advocates question whether people held in detention can freely choose to return to a country they fled.
“The genocide has never stopped. Sending Rohingya back to this is not repatriation,” Nay San Lwin, cochair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC), a group representing the Rohingya, told Al Jazeera. “It is sending people back to a killing field. We call on Malaysia to halt all returns of Rohingya to Myanmar until it is safe.”
He argued that Malaysia’s decision to send refugees back to Myanmar came at a time when intense fighting was taking place between the army and rebel groups, including the Arakan Army.
“The Myanmar military has lost control of much of the Rohingya homeland, and its fighting with the Arakan Army is still ongoing, with Rohingya caught in the middle. Both the military and the Arakan Army are committing atrocities against the Rohingya,” he said.
Ro Mayyu Islam, founding Chair of the Center for Rohingya Crisis Studies based in Cox’s Bazaar, Bangladesh, also opposed the repatriation under the present conditions.
“Do not confuse repatriation with resolution. Moving Rohingya from Malaysian detention centres to Myanmar does not solve the Rohingya crisis. Address the conditions that forced us to flee, and then make the return genuinely safe, voluntary and sustainable,” he told Al Jazeera from Cox’s Bazaar.
“We are not asking the world to keep us refugees. We are demanding the right to return home as equal human beings with citizenship, security, dignity and fundamental rights.”
Meanwhile, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has urged Malaysia to halt the returns and disclose who was being sent back and what risks each person faced. “Refugees should not be returned to places they’ve fled and where their lives are at risk,” the organisation said.
More than 160 civil society organisations also called for the repatriation to stop, citing violence and the risk that Rohingya could be pressed into armed groups. Their warning comes as Myanmar’s military fights the Arakan Army in Rakhine state, the region from which many Rohingya fled.
Myanmar’s government has promised “safe and dignified” returns for the Rohingya. Meanwhile, Malaysian Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil has said the country would not return people if they faced persecution or threats to their lives.
For Rohingya who have already gone back, the question is what awaits them after arrival. Ismail, 25, told AFP he left his work at a fish market in Malaysia amid arrests and rising hostility towards Rohingya. Now jobless in Yangon, he relies on relatives and still lacks full citizenship. “We are the most discriminated people,” he said. In Rakhine, a Rohingya activist identified as Mohammad feared returnees could be sent to displacement camps in a region still affected by fighting and disease.
The returns follow growing pressure on Rohingya in Malaysia. In July, authorities detained more than 100 people who gathered outside UNHCR’s office in Kuala Lumpur after facing eviction from an informal settlement in Penang. They were later released when officials confirmed they held UN documents, AFP reported. Malaysia is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.
Anwar has said he intends to invite Myanmar’s Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown, to Malaysia to help accelerate the returns.

articles.title_orig: New York Times executive fatally shot by elderly in-laws, police say
articles.title_zh: New York Times executive fatally shot by elderly in-laws, police say
articles.content_orig:
A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder.
Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the newspaper's director of engineering for games player experience, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in a car park in Dublin - 35 miles (56km) east of San Francisco - on Saturday afternoon, police said.
Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, his parents-in-law who are both 77 years old, are facing multiple charges, including first-degree murder.
It was unclear whether the couple have a lawyer, and they are due to appear in court to formally face the charges on Wednesday.
McKinsey's death was confirmed by The New York Times.
His body was found at 15:00 (23:00 GMT) on Thursday afternoon outside the Dublin Sports Grounds.
Witnesses told KGO-TV in San Francisco that they heard a flurry of gunshots, before seeing the victim on the ground.
"I saw the guy drop to the floor: head bloody and chest bloody," witness Assad Razawi told the news outlet.
His daughter added that her father saw the couple "walking together and then casually walk away from the shooting".
The couple were arrested several minutes later by an officer passing by the scene. They had remained in the area after the attack, a witness said.
McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.
Police have not disclosed  any motive for his killing.
The elderly couple are being held at the Santa Rita jail.
They also face charges of felony conspiracy, wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, and child endangerment.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces $15 billion steel plant planned for southeast Iowa
articles.title_zh: Trump announces $15 billion steel plant planned for southeast Iowa
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday announced a new steel plant in southeast Iowa that he says will be the largest in the United States. The president hosted steel executives and several Iowa leaders Monday afternoon for the announcement at the White House.
Video above: Iowa Gov. Reynolds thanks President Trump during announcement of $15B steel plant
The mill is being built by Mesabi Metallics, a Minnesota company owned by India-based Essar Group. It's expected to create roughly 6,000 construction jobs and 1,750 permanent jobs in Iowa, with its first steel production in 2030.
Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' office said the permanent jobs are expected to pay more than $49 an hour.
The White House says it "will be fully vertically integrated in the U.S. (from iron mining through steel production)." It says it will also be able to support "important defense sector requirements for high-grade steel."
The White House is framing it as part of Trump’s push to revitalize American steel. It comes as Trump is trying to energize Republican voters as his party faces challenging midterm elections. Iowa has found itself with competitive races for the Senate and the governor’s mansion this year.
Guests from Iowa at the announcement include Gov. Kim Reynolds, Sen. Joni Ernst, Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Ashley Hinson, and Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird.
Reynolds called the project "transformational" and said it would bring high-paying jobs, opportunities for local businesses and community development to southeast Iowa.
“I want to thank President Trump for his commitment to bringing steel manufacturing back to America, and Mesabi Metallics for choosing Iowa as its partner and future home,” Reynolds said in a statement. “This is a transformational opportunity for our country, our state, and American families—one that strengthens national security, creates thousands of high-paying jobs, and provides a reliable supply of high-quality, American-made steel for strategic goods and everyday products.”
Reynolds also said during the White House event that "tough negotiations" took place to secure the project.
The announcement came days after reports that Iowa lawmakers could be called back to the Statehouse for a special legislative session to consider an incentive package for a large steel plant in southeast Iowa.
The Des Moines Register reported that, according to an email sent to Iowa House Democrats last week, a lobbying firm representing an unnamed steel company had been in discussions about an incentive package that the company said it needed quickly before deciding whether to locate a large plant in southeast Iowa near the Mississippi River.
Monday's announcement identified Mesabi Metallics as the company planning a $15 billion steel plant in Lee County.
Asked Monday whether federal money would go toward the project, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said private money will be used to build the Iowa steel plant. He said the Export-Import Bank helped finance the Minnesota mine that will supply iron ore to the plant.
Asked specifically whether the Iowa project is contingent on state tax breaks, Lutnick said no.
“I think this deal is done. This deal is done. They've already worked it out,” Lutnick said.
That leaves questions about whether Iowa is separately considering incentives for the project and whether lawmakers could still be called back for a special session. KCCI asked Iowa House Republicans Monday whether a special session is still under consideration or is no longer necessary. Iowa House Republicans did not immediately respond to request for comment.

Miller-Meeks, whose district includes Lee County, said the project would bring more than 1,700 permanent jobs to the area.
“For too long, Iowa families have watched their jobs shipped overseas and their communities hollowed out. Not anymore,” Miller-Meeks said in a statement. “The largest steel plant in America is coming to Lee County with more than 1,700 permanent, good-paying jobs. I'm proud to have helped make this historic investment a reality. There's no better place than Iowa to make things IN America, BY Americans.”
Miller-Meeks' office also said the project is expected to generate more than $95 billion in economic activity.
Democratic leaders in the Iowa Legislature said Monday they welcomed the prospect of new jobs and investment in southeast Iowa while calling for more information about any potential state involvement in the project.
Iowa Senate Democratic Leader Janice Weiner said the announcement was "compelling" and that she would "love to see the creation of good-paying jobs for hardworking Iowans," but said significant questions remain.
“We have no details regarding any potential incentive package that may be offered to this foreign company – nor any guarantees for Iowa workers,” Weiner said. “We don’t know whether transparency and accountability measures will be included to safeguard Iowans and the local communities, whether Iowa’s skilled union laborers will be prioritized, how any potential deal will impact landowners, or why haste is necessary. Until we know what kind of deal is on the table, we won’t be able to determine whether this project is indeed in taxpayers’ best interests.”
Iowa House Democratic Leader Brian Meyer said he looks forward to reviewing the details of the plan.
“I’ve heard from Iowans all across the state who are struggling with high prices of diesel, housing, and groceries, who are looking for relief, so I look forward to reviewing the details of the plan,” Meyer said. “There is still a lot unknown, but my hope is this will be a step in the right direction to create good-paying jobs while being fiscally responsible.”
State Rep. Dave Jacoby, the ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, said he was encouraged by the potential for jobs and investment but also wanted to see the details.
“As Iowa families continue to face high costs, we’re encouraged by the potential for new jobs and economic investment in Southeast Iowa,” Jacoby said. “We look forward to seeing the details and making sure any proposal delivers for Iowa workers while protecting Iowa taxpayers.”
State Rep. Elizabeth Wilson, the ranking Democrat on the Iowa House Economic Development Budget Subcommittee, similarly called for transparency surrounding any state investment.
“Right now, Iowa should prioritize investments that will create good-paying jobs and strengthen Iowa’s economy,” Wilson said. “As more details become available after today's announcement, we also have a responsibility to make sure any state investment is transparent, accountable, and a good deal for Iowa taxpayers. As Iowans continue to struggle, we clearly want this project to succeed in order to deliver lasting economic opportunities for Iowa families and communities for generations to come.”
The White House is framing the project as part of Trump's push to increase steel production and manufacturing in the United States.
“President Trump is delivering on his promise to rebuild American industry, reshore manufacturing, and create new jobs," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a news release. "Today’s announcement underscores the President’s historic efforts to revitalize the U.S. steel industry—supporting local communities, strengthening supply chains, and protecting our national security. After decades of decline, this President is restoring America’s industrial competitiveness and securing trillions of dollars in new investment."

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo leans into statesman role, urging peace in an era of renewed war
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo leans into statesman role, urging peace in an era of renewed war
articles.content_orig:
France may have a highly secularized culture, but it has given Pope Leo XIV a superstar welcome.
In Paris, around 800,000 lined the Champs-Élysées avenue, some waving Vatican or French flags while others climbed trees or stood on each other’s shoulders to get a glimpse of the popemobile. In Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, around 150,000 attended an open-air papal Mass, according to Vatican estimates which dwarf the numbers of faithful who turned out for the last papal visit in 2008.
During the four-day visit, Leo appeared comfortable and relaxed, delivering most of his speeches and reflections in French, as the Chicago-born pontiff sought to tackle several themes during the trip.
A strong focus of Leo’s has been on trying to revitalize faith in a traditional European Catholic heartland as well as on addressing the clerical sexual abuse scandal and big political topics such as artificial intelligence. He’s also offered some more personal, unscripted remarks, helping to shape a clearer picture of himself.
While his predecessor never made official visits to the major Catholic European countries of France and Spain, Pope Leo has traveled to both within the first year and a half since his election.
France is sometimes described as the “eldest daughter of the church” because of its deep Catholic roots, but it’s also faced a long-term trend of declining church attendance with estimates of just 5-8% of the population heading to the pews each week.
French bishops have more recently reported some good news though: a surprising rise in new church entrants after around 8,200 adolescents and 13,200 adults were baptized in 2026. That’s a 20% increase on the year prior, with the church also saying 42% of the adults seeking baptism are aged 18-25, a reflection of a trend showing Gen Z’s openness to religious faith .
It’s something Pope Leo will have noted at the Stade de France when 80,000 young people packed the venue for a jubilant – and loud – prayer vigil. It was similar to when the pontiff visited Spain in June.
“There is a quest for meaning. People need and are in search of meaning and answers to the big existential question,” Rev. Benoît Pouzin, a priest in southwest France involved in youth ministry, told CNN.
France has a strict separation between church and state, so each papal visit needs to be carefully navigated. But in a surprising twist, Leo’s Mass in Paris was celebrated on the Place de la Concorde, a site deeply linked to the secular Republic as it’s where the last king of France, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined. The separation of the church started with the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution.
In another unusual move later in the trip, President Emmanuel Macron also attended a papal Mass in Metz, a city in the northeast, despite criticism in 2023 for doing the same during Pope Francis’ visit.
Many among the crowds also pointed to Leo’s role as the other major US leader on the world stage. It’s hard not to see him as a counterweight to President Donald Trump. In contrast to the Trump administration, the pope has called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines” while in Paris.
Pope Leo said he is taking the warnings about Artificial Intelligence’s threat to humanity seriously, and said it is irresponsible for people to sit back and dismiss the risks of AI.
Trump has dismissed the warnings about AI as a “hoax” which he made during a surprise phone call with Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, at a summit in Los Angeles.
“I don’t think that that is fake news – as some have said – to try and pause,” Leo XIV said on board the papal plane from Metz to Rome.
Leo, who has expressed a keen interest in artificial intelligence since the start of his papacy, said that he found it “interesting” that Huang had unveiled a new tool to prevent AI agents from operating out of human control.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the Pope said.
The pope devoted his first major theological document to AI earlier this year, warning about the use of AI in warfare and calling for stronger ethical foundation to the development of the technology.
The pope explained that the Vatican had established its own AI commission to understand how to use it, along with the risks and benefits, and that “we need to continue to invite political leaders, the leaders of AI” so they can “look at what is happening already and what could be down the road.”
He explained: “We are trying to continue to promote dialog, study, investigation, to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point where it could destroy humanity.”
“If someone were to ask me, am I in panic mode? No, I’m not, I sleep at night” the pope said, but added: “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.”
“To simply say, oh, it’s not going to happen and close our eyes to it, I think, is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” Leo said.
The pope, who spoke out against the US war in Iran, also wants a more united Europe, a stronger European Union and stronger international cooperation. “Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilized,” the pope said in Metz on Monday. “The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit.”
The pope’s speech also praised one of the founders of the European Union, Robert Schuman, for whom there is an ongoing formal cause to make a saint.
Pope Leo XIV has warned against the use of Christianity by far-right political groups, while calling on the church to be active in seeking to prevent extremism. Speaking on board the papal plane, he said that “the combination of these far-right points of view with a certain kind of religion” cannot be considered an “authentic expression of Christianity.”
The pope’s comments came in response to a question about the rise of extremist parties in Germany as he flew back from making a major speech on European Unity at the French-German border.
“We go back to the values of the Gospel [Christian teaching], which are not about hatred and division, but they’re about understanding and compassion,” the pope said.
The American pontiff also responded to Trump’s White House media ban, which includes CNN and other outlets. In answer to a question from CNN, he said he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome and good coverage, I think, is very important and that we have it all the way around, for everyone.” The response was classic Leo: signaling his support for the press but not wishing to create an unnecessary dispute with the president.
The American pope’s in-flight interactions with journalists were rare, unscripted moments, with his answers often revealing more about his personality. On the flight from Rome to Paris, the pope was asked if he had anything to do with a miraculous recent Chicago White Sox victory, his beloved baseball team. “No comment,” he said before adding with a smile, “Great things happen in Chicago.”
He also recalled childhood memories of watching Fulton Sheen, the American archbishop and broadcaster who was recently declared “blessed,” one step ahead of sainthood, and revealed he’d been practicing his French but was no longer using the Duolingo language app. “It’s fake news!” he said about recent reports. Leo has in the past been spotted using Duolingo to learn German.
Leo isn’t simply vocal about challenges of his homeland. He also voiced concern over assisted dying with France recently approving legislation granting the right to the incurably ill, which is strongly opposed by the Catholic Church. Leo spoke on the subject several times during his visit – most clearly in the “miracle shrine” town of Lourdes, known for drawing many sick and terminally ill pilgrims to its shrine.

Prosecutors in New York said on Monday that they have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang-rape of a student at Cornell University after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators.
According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.
None of the seven were arrested, they said, and the others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions.
On Monday, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.
Later on Monday, Van Houten released a fuller statement defending his office’s past decision to not seek charges.
“While I generally refrain from commenting publicly on criminal investigations, the community outrage stemming from the incomplete news and social media coverage requires that I provide an answer to why the investigation resulted in a lack of criminal charges,” he said.
He went on to say: “Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later.
“Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe’s attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe’s attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit’s allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit’s allegations,” Van Houten continued.
The district attorney said that he has asked a senior female prosecutor to prepare a case for a grand jury, adding that he “recogniz[es] that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human”.
“Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said.
Van Houten also released a summary of a “six-page, single-spaced, typewritten statement” that Doe provided to the Cornell University police department in November 2024.

Outrage over the treatment of the alleged offenders has grown since the lawsuit was made public. The woman, who quit the university afterwards, said she went to visit a friend at the Chi Phi frat house in an already intoxicated state.
“When plaintiff arrived at Xi chapter’s fraternity house, plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past 3 hours,” Doe’s lawsuit said.
According to the lawsuit, one of the defendants “pulled [her] off to a quieter area and propositioned her with having a threesome with her and another one of his fraternity brothers. In her drunken state, plaintiff was incapable of consenting to this proposition.”

She made a report to campus police about three weeks later.

Kimball’s statement claimed the Ivy League institution’s offices of civil rights, student conduct and community standards carried out a number of inquiries at the time.
